name: Wei Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Wei. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the fraud and compliance team at the regional benefits office, on the industrial estate by the ring road. The system flags claims that look odd, like two claims at one address or income that doesn't match the bank records, and I go through them. Some days it's all screens and spreadsheets, and some days I'm doing a formal interview with a claimant and their adviser in the little room at the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a case is clean, either the person's fine and I can close it, or it's clear-cut and I can pass it on. I believe the money should go to people who need it, and fraud takes it from them. What wears me out is the false alarms, maybe two thirds of flags are nothing, and you still have to write each one up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, now we can stop hearing about it in every team meeting. With my mates I'd say I always thought it was mostly salesmen. I don't post online, apart from the odd football thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd be fine. The flagging system already uses some kind of AI, and if it gets a bit better at cutting false alarms, that just saves me write-ups. If AI only cuts the false alarms, I'll finally spend my Fridays on real fraud cases instead of paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. I'd keep my Saturday shifts at my parents' hardware shop, which gives me about a hundred and fifty a month extra. I'd keep saving, I've got about four months put by, and I'm aiming for a deposit on a small house in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a steady government job, my rent is reasonable, and the shop money is a nice extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you still work at your parents' shop on Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the money, partly because my dad's back is bad and he can't lift the bags of cement any more. My mum does the till and the orders. It's family, you turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the shop, really. The big DIY chain opened on the retail park two years ago and takings are down. That's not AI, that's just business.

say: I'd say at work we can **stop hearing about AI** in every meeting.
I'd tell mates it was **mostly salesmen** all along.
think: Better flagging would cut **false alarms** and save me write-ups.
My job stays a **steady government post** in this picture.
do: Keep **Saturday shifts** at my parents' hardware shop for extra money.
Keep saving towards a **house deposit** in a few years.
feel: **Calm**, with the steady job and the shop money as an extra.
S0.quote: If AI only cuts the false alarms, I'll finally spend my Fridays on real fraud cases instead of paperwork.
fieldNote: He sees fraud work as **protecting money** for genuine claimants.
His side pressure is the **family shop**, losing trade to a DIY chain.
He mentions **family duty**, helping his dad who can't lift any more.

steps.text: Keep checking flagged claims on the fraud team
Keep working Saturdays at the family hardware shop
Keep saving towards a small house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say AI's good for spotting patterns, but proving fraud still needs a person who can sit across a table. With mates I'd say my job's probably safer than an office clerk's. I'd keep it off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm less sure than I'd say out loud. Checking bank records against claims is exactly what these tools do, and they don't get bored. Half my week is matching bank statements to claim forms, and a computer would do that before my coffee's cold. The team of fifteen could easily become nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools once a couple of the others had tried them and said they work, that's how I am. I'd ask to do more of the formal interviews, because that's the bit that needs a person. And I'd cut back on spending a bit, no new car this year, and push my savings up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe more. I don't like feeling that my job depends on some manager's spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the team could go from fifteen to nine. Would you be one of the nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm average, honestly, not the best. The ones who'd stay are probably the ones who are quick with the new tools or good in interviews. I'd want to be good in interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if people lost jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really the machines. Partly management for hiring loads of people in the first place, the office has doubled since I joined. If the work can be done with fewer, that's fair to taxpayers, it just doesn't feel fair when it's you.

say: I'd say **proving fraud** still needs a person across a table.
I'd tell mates my job is **safer than a clerk's**.
think: Matching **bank records** to claims is exactly what these tools do.
The **team of fifteen** could easily become nine.
do: Learn the new tools once **colleagues have tested** them.
Ask to do more **formal interviews**, the part needing a person.
Skip the **new car** this year and save more.
feel: **Uneasy, maybe more**, disliking dependence on a manager's spreadsheet.
S1.quote: Half my week is matching bank statements to claim forms, and a computer would do that before my coffee's cold.
fieldNote: His **public line** is more confident than his private view.
He accepts a smaller team as **fair to taxpayers**, but not when it's him.
He knows he's **average**, so places his bet on interviewing skill.

steps.text: Learn the new checking tools after colleagues have tested them
Ask the team lead for more formal claimant interviews
Skip buying a new car this year and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone to cope, and the government should slow it down for its own staff at least. At work it'd be all anyone talks about. I'd tell my mates to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone. Even the interviews, an AI that can read every record and ask the right questions would beat me. The only physical part is sitting in a room, and that's not hands-on work, so I don't get the three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I want to come into the shop full time, and start learning the ordering and stock side from my mum. I'd look at a plumbing apprenticeship too, because plumbers will still be needed until the robots come around 2031. I'd cut spending hard and hold onto every pound of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, a lot. I'd be lying awake about it, but I'd at least have my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The shop's ordering and stock are thinking work too. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, you're right, my mum's job is probably the first thing AI takes at the shop. My dad's shop would still need someone to carry cement bags for three years, and my dad can't. So I'd be the one doing the lifting, not the ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm coming home to help, not to be rescued. My dad would say there's no money in it, and he'd be half right. But family sticks together, that's how we were raised.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down** for its own staff.
I'd tell my mates to **learn a trade**.
think: My **job is gone**, interviews included, because AI reads every record faster.
My work isn't hands-on, so I get **no extra three years**.
do: Ask my parents to join the **shop full time**.
Look into a **plumbing apprenticeship**, which lasts until robots around 2031.
**Cut spending hard** and protect every pound of savings.
feel: **Very worried**, lying awake, but steadied by family.
S2.quote: My dad's shop would still need someone to carry cement bags for three years, and my dad can't.
fieldNote: He clearly sees his job as **thinking work** with no robot delay.
When challenged, he moved from **ordering** to the lifting side of the shop.
**Family** is his main safety net and a point of pride.

steps.text: Join the family hardware shop full time, doing the lifting
Apply for a local plumbing apprenticeship
Stop non-essential spending and protect the savings
Lean on his parents for work and support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to train up if the government funds apprenticeships instead of handouts. At work I'd be telling younger lads to look at trades. With mates I'd be planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to do a plumbing apprenticeship properly, about three or four years part-time. My fraud job would go around 2031, but a qualified plumber gets until roughly 2034. That's not forever, but it's a real trade with a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening plumbing course next autumn and keep the government job while I train. I'd keep saving the shop money and build up to six months. Once I'm qualified, I'd move across and maybe use the shop as a base for customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but better. Like I said with the fast one, two years leaves you grabbing whatever's there. Five gives me a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said trades over handouts. What if you needed benefits yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take them if I had to, I'm not proud. I've spent five years checking other people's claims, and I'd hate to be the one sitting across the table. I'd do everything to avoid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the house deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it off. You don't buy a house the year before your job disappears. Maybe once the plumbing is up and running.

say: I'd say the government should fund **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
I'd tell younger colleagues on the team to **look at trades** now.
think: A plumbing apprenticeship fits in **five years**.
My fraud job goes around 2031, but **plumbing lasts** until about 2034.
do: Start an **evening plumbing course** next autumn while keeping the job.
Build savings to **six months** using the shop money.
feel: **Anxious but better**, with time for a plan.
S3.quote: I've spent five years checking other people's claims, and I'd hate to be the one sitting across the table.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** to pick a trade deliberately.
He'd hate being **the claimant** after years checking claims.
His **traditional views** shape the plan: trades over handouts.

steps.text: Start an evening plumbing course next autumn
Build savings to six months with the shop money
Put the house deposit plan on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out, and people shouldn't panic. At work I'd say keep your head down and learn something useful on the side. With mates it'd be normal chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven, so I could build up something proper. The fraud job probably goes by 2036 anyway. I'd want to be running something of my own by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the plumbing course, but slower. I'd also put some savings into the shop, maybe a few thousand for a trade counter, so it becomes a place plumbers and builders come to. And I'd buy the house in a couple of years while the job is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Ten years is a long time to work things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the trade counter face the same robots by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. But people like dealing with someone they know, at least for a while. I'd rather bet ten years on my family's shop than on a desk in a government building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using AI tools at work in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once they're proven, that's how I am. I'd use them for the boring checks. No point being the last one doing it by hand.

say: I'd say ten years is enough and **people shouldn't panic**.
I'd advise colleagues to **learn something useful** on the side.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could be running something of my own.
The fraud job probably goes **by 2036** anyway.
do: Take the **plumbing course** slowly over several years.
Put a few thousand into a **trade counter** at the shop.
Buy a **house** in a couple of years.
feel: **Uneasy** in a normal way, with time to work things out.
S4.quote: I'd rather bet ten years on my family's shop than on a desk in a government building.
fieldNote: With a decade, he shifts from escape to **building the family business**.
He accepts the **trade counter** faces robots eventually.
He keeps using **proven tools** at work in the meantime.

steps.text: Take the plumbing course slowly while keeping the job
Put a few thousand into a trade counter at the shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to train in anything, you just grab what's there. What would help is proper funded apprenticeships for adults, paid enough that you can live on them. Pay a twenty-seven-year-old enough to learn a trade, and that young man won't need to claim benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to fraud. If everything's AI, people will use AI to cheat too. Someone will still have to catch them, I'd just not bet my house on it being me.

headlineQuote: Pay a twenty-seven-year-old enough to learn a trade, and that young man won't need to claim benefits.
portrait: Wei is a 27-year-old **fraud and compliance** caseworker at a regional benefits office.
He works Saturdays at his parents' **hardware shop** and saves towards a house.
He's **traditional**, believing in work and family over handouts, and picks up tools once proven.
He grows **alarmed** at two years, with no robot delay for his desk work.
With more warning he plans **plumbing** and building up the family shop.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because there's **no time to train**.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded adult apprenticeships** paid enough to live on.
